cim: At Woodstock Day School, Students and Parents Grapple With AI’s Place in Their Future
cim_eredeti: At Woodstock Day School, Students and Parents Grapple With AI’s Place in Their Future
szoveg_eredeti:
Will Fox wants to study film in college. The Woodstock Day School senior worries that artificial intelligence could upend the career he hopes to pursue.

Those concerns surfaced one evening before bed, prompting his mother, Eve Fox, a trustee at the school, to help organize a community discussion about AI.

“It’s something that I have almost no control over,” Will Fox, 17, said.“And I think the biggest problem right now is that people don’t think that it’s a problem really; but it could take away our future.”

Parents, educators, students, and other community members gathered Nov. 15 at Woodstock Day School, the small private school in Saugerties for an “AI Reality Check” watch party and discussion led by Head of School Ashley Hughes. The school enrolls about 180 students from nursery school through 12th grade, according to its website.

The discussion comes as school districts across The Overlook’s coverage area try to set rules for AI tools that students and teachers are already using. Their approaches range from formal policies to teacher guidance and plagiarism rules, while students seek clearer boundaries and question what the technology means for their future careers.

The group watched a recorded presentation from Humans in Control, an advocacy organization seeking stronger rules for AI companies.

For Fox and his classmate Luca Kaufman, 16, those questions were already part of daily school life. Interviewed after the event, they said students understood they couldn’t use AI to write their assignments, but described a less certain boundary around research, grammar checks, and help understanding homework.

The two said they actively tried not to use AI. They also described classroom discussions about whether work had been generated by AI, and said some teachers used the technology, too. What they wanted was clearer guidance about what was acceptable.

Kaufman, who’s considering studying political science or history, said he noticed ChatGPT open on many students’ computer screens while walking through the library during a summer program at Columbia University.

Fox worried that students could spend years earning a degree and developing skills only to find that the work they had trained for had changed or disappeared. They could, he said, “learn all this stuff just for it to be completely arbitrary in the future and completely useless.” The usefulness adults found in AI, he said, could obscure how threatening its future felt to young people just preparing to enter the workforce.

College Board reported that 84% of high school students it surveyed used generative AI for schoolwork in May 2025, up from 79% in January.

Fox worried that years spent earning a degree and developing skills could leave students prepared for work that had changed or disappeared. They could, he said, “learn all this stuff just for it to be completely arbitrary in the future and completely useless.”

The Day School is looking to create a formal AI policy, with students’ input.

“I think that where we are right now as a school is wanting to hear from the students,” Hughes said. “How are you using it?”

Rules would have limits, she said, when students could use the same tools outside school.

Schools are working out AI’s limits as New York expands its investment in the technology. Gov. Kathy Hochul broke ground Thursday on Empire AI’s permanent home at the University at Buffalo. The supercomputer is shared by New York universities.

Formal rules vary widely. An Oct. 13 analysis by New York Focus found that more than half of New York’s 678 school districts lacked formal, board-adopted AI policies.

At Onteora’s Nov. 17 board meeting, trustee Rick Knutsen shared what he’d heard at the Day School event as members discussed reviewing the district’s AI policy, adopted Aug. 18.

Onteora’s student guidance allows approved tools with teachers’ permission and requires students to verify AI’s output and take responsibility for their work. Administrators sent educators and families a practical guide in September.

Knutsen, responding as an individual trustee, called policy development “an iterative process.” Members had discussed an ad hoc committee and public forum, he said, with no firm timetable for next steps.

Saugerties adopted a policy on Jan. 14, 2025, that leaves student use to individual teachers, who must explain their expectations and discuss AI’s risks. Students are responsible for the accuracy of their work.

Windham-Ashland-Jewett’s technology plan lists ChatGPT among tools teachers can use to adapt assignments for English language learners. Hunter-Tannersville doesn’t yet have an AI policy and aims to complete one by the end of the 2026-27 school year. Kingston, which serves some Hurley residents, includes AI in its code of conduct’s definition of plagiarism.

Knutsen also urged rules for the companies supplying the technology. He said he wrote a resolution the New York State School Boards Association adopted Oct. 15, calling for legislation requiring companies that provide student AI products to meet safety and privacy standards and take reasonable steps to prevent foreseeable harm to children.

The association also sought notice when updates add AI features and an option for schools to opt out. The votes set lobbying priorities; they didn’t enact laws.

Late in the discussion, Hughes asked participants to hold up fingers indicating how scared, angry, and sad they felt on a scale of one to five. Many fours and fives shot up.

“I think we left them at sea,” Hughes said of children’s experience with social media. “So I’m hoping that we can do it a little bit differently and a little bit better this go around.”

Noah Eckstein is the editor-in-chief of The Overlook. Send correspondence to noah@theoverlooknews.com.
